what_its_for: Methimazole is used to treat an overactive thyroid gland (called hyperthyroidism). Your thyroid gland makes too much thyroid hormone, which can cause a fast heartbeat, weight loss, sweating, and feeling nervous or anxious. This medicine helps slow down your thyroid so it makes less hormone and brings your levels back to normal.
how_to_take: Take methimazole by mouth with or without food. Try to take it at the same time(s) every day. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. If the tablet is hard to swallow, you may crush it and mix it with a small amount of soft food or water. Do not stop taking this medicine on your own, even if you feel better — stopping suddenly can make your condition worse.
dosing: Your doctor will set your dose based on how overactive your thyroid is. A typical starting dose for adults is 15 to 60 mg per day, often split into doses taken every 8 hours. As your thyroid levels improve, your doctor will likely lower your dose to a maintenance level, usually 5 to 15 mg per day. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Never double up or take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store methimazole at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use the medicine past the expiration date printed on the package.
what_to_avoid: Avoid taking iodine supplements or eating very large amounts of iodine-rich foods (like kelp or seaweed) unless your doctor says it is okay, as iodine can affect how well this medicine works. Tell your doctor or dentist about all medicines you take, including blood thinners (like warfarin), because methimazole can interact with them. Do not get any vaccines without checking with your doctor first. Avoid activities that could increase your risk of infection, since this medicine can lower your ability to fight infections.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you notice any of these warning signs: fever, chills, sore throat, or mouth sores (these could be signs of a very serious drop in white blood cells called agranulocytosis); unusual bleeding or bruising; yellowing of your skin or eyes (jaundice); dark-colored urine; severe stomach pain; skin rash or itching; joint pain or swelling; or numbness or tingling. Also call your doctor if you feel unusually tired, gain weight unexpectedly, feel very cold, or develop new or worsening symptoms.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within 1 to 2 weeks of starting methimazole, but it usually takes 4 to 8 weeks for your thyroid hormone levels to return to normal. Some people need to take this medicine for 1 to 2 years. Your doctor will check your thyroid levels with blood tests regularly to make sure the medicine is working correctly and adjust your dose as needed.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Methimazole is generally NOT recommended during the first trimester of pregnancy because it may cause rare birth defects. A different medicine (propylthiouracil) is usually used in early pregnancy. Tell your doctor right away if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Breastfeeding: This medicine can pass into breast milk and may affect your baby's thyroid. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Children: Methimazole can be used in children, but the dose will be much lower and carefully adjusted by the doctor. Elderly patients: No major dose changes are usually needed, but close monitoring is still important.
